game.name: Darkest Dungeon®
game.short_description: Darkest Dungeon is a challenging gothic roguelike turn-based RPG about the psychological stresses of adventuring. Recruit, train, and lead a team of flawed heroes against unimaginable horrors, stress, disease, and the ever-encroaching dark. Can you keep your heroes together when all hope is lost?

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Darkest Dungeon is a turn-based dungeon crawler where you send a party from a village hub into dungeons, with permadeath on characters you may have invested 10+ hours in. He describes it as the Dark Souls of roguelikes in terms of how brutal and devastating it can feel. He finds a recurring cycle: play, lose a favourite character, quit for a long time, then return. He respects it and comes back now and then, but finds it too brutal for his taste and places it in mid B tier.
praise: Turn-based combat is fun and engaging
Village hub with new recruits and upgrades gives a strong progression loop
Distinctive reputation for punishing, high-stakes difficulty that some players love
Emotional attachment to characters you level up over many hours
He keeps returning to it periodically
criticism: Heavy RNG: bosses can crit and wipe out a character, or a character randomly gets sick
Permadeath of a long-invested character feels terrible and makes him want to stop
Balance issues, even if partly intentional to feel bad
Items often have downsides as big as their upsides and feel useless, so building a character is hard beyond levels and currency
unique_points: Deliberately makes you feel terrible; the balance issues are part of the intended gameplay
Long-term investment in individual characters combined with permadeath creates a distinctive emotional cycle
Uses a strong character to help level up a weaker team
commentary.quote: I think it's a little too brutal for me
design_criteria: Difficulty and RNG: heavy randomness can feel unfair and devastating
Permadeath stakes: losing a heavily invested character drives him away
Meta-progression: village upgrades and recruits give progression
Itemization: items with equal upsides and downsides limit build crafting
Balance: issues exist but are partly intentional
Combat style: turn-based aspect is enjoyable

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Darkest Dungeon is a turn-based dungeon crawler with permanent character death, where your roster persists across missions instead of resetting each run. He rated it B about a year and a half earlier because it felt too punishing, but after revisiting it and seeing how influential it is in the genre, he raised it sharply. He now places it in a very high A, acknowledging some would say S. What holds it back from S for him is the heavy punishment and time commitment, and he admits he has never finished it.
praise: Permadeath of long-invested characters is a rare and bold twist on the genre, and it is the whole point of the game
Stress meter and psychological breakdowns (anxious, abusive) are unique and make you care about your characters
Boss fights feel incredibly rewarding and nerve-wracking because you can lose your favorite team, compared to early Souls boss victories
Deep strategy that rewards knowledge, roster management and swapping characters
Strong sense of adventure pushing toward the final dungeon and final boss
Fantastic tense, dark music and great art style
The narrator is iconic and makes the game very immersive
criticism: Very punishing and hard, losing a character you have invested in to a random crit or miss stings
Combines permadeath with notable luck, which can feel rough
Requires a big time and dedication commitment to reach the end; he has not finished it
His own earlier experience was dying and wanting to quit, so it is not for the faint of heart
unique_points: Permadeath applies to persistent characters rather than whole runs, so progression is not classic roguelike reset
Stress and psychology system where characters crack under pressure and you must manage it
Design philosophy of dealing with the worst case and not giving up, embracing dying and repeating
Narrator that comments on everything happening in the game
commentary.quote: I'm going to leave it as a high A for me.
design_criteria: Risk vs reward: permadeath and luck-influenced crits create high stakes, weighed against punishment
Meta-progression: persistent roster with levels and abilities carried between missions
Difficulty: very hard and punishing, which costs it an S for him
Strategy depth: rewards knowledge and roster management
Enemy/boss design: bosses are tense, high-stakes payoffs
Audio: tense, dark music and iconic narrator
Visuals/theme: great art and world-building, characters and story
Run length/commitment: long time investment to finish
Unique mechanics: stress and psychology system
commentary.rerank_note: Re-evaluation: he rated it B in his original tier list about a year and a half earlier as too punishing, and now bumps it from a mid B to a very high A.

community.one_liner: A gothic, Lovecraft-flavoured turn-based party RPG by Red Hook Studios where you run a roster of flawed heroes through procedurally assembled dungeons, managing both health and mental stress, with permanent death and a hamlet hub that carries progress between expeditions.
community.consensus_summary: Darkest Dungeon is widely regarded as a modern classic of the genre: about 91.7% of roughly 163k Steam reviews are positive (Very Positive), Metacritic sits at 84 and OpenCritic at 84 with about 93% of critics recommending it. Critics and players praise the art, narrator, stress system and tense, consequential party tactics. The recurring complaint is that the late game turns into a grind, compounded by swingy RNG (back-to-back crits, surprise ambushes) that can wipe out heroes you spent hours levelling. It was in Steam Early Access from Jan 2015 and launched fully on 19 Jan 2016, and it is still being updated: a new DLC, The Fire's Edge, appears in current Steam data. Sequel Darkest Dungeon II (Steam appid 1940340) is a different, more run-based roguelite structure.
best_things: Distinctive gothic storybook art direction and Lovecraftian atmosphere that critics and players call hauntingly beautiful
Wayne June's narrator performance and the audio/music, repeatedly singled out as elevating every expedition
The stress/affliction system: mental health as a second resource that creates emergent story moments and meaningful risk
Tactical turn-based combat built around rank positioning, with deep hero class variety, quirks, and team synergies
High stakes and permadeath make every decision, victory, and loss feel weighty; 'easy to learn, hard to master' as one long-time player puts it
Hamlet hub progression gives persistence even when heroes die, so failure still moves the meta forward
Rewarding loot and trinket hunting, lots of bosses and dungeon variety, plus a large modding scene
Strong content additions over time (The Crimson Court, The Color of Madness, The Butcher's Circus PvP arena)
worst_things: Late-game grind: players feel they must repeatedly farm low-level dungeons to replace fallen heroes before attempting the Darkest Dungeon itself
RNG swinginess: chains of enemy crits, missed high-accuracy attacks, and turn-order variance can undo 20 hours of progress
Hero level restrictions that bar a stronger hero from easier quests, which forces awkward roster juggling and farming
Quests are slow (20 to 60 minutes) with slow animations and back-and-forth map movement, so the game can feel like it does not respect player time
Knowledge-check design: you often learn a boss or curio mechanic only by dying to it, so many players lean on wikis and guides

Heavy economy drain from stress relief, disease cures, quirk removal, provisions and expensive final gear upgrades (for example thousands of gold per top-tier weapon, 100+ deeds mentioned by one forum poster)
Some reviewers found the stress acting-out and Crimson Curse systems annoying, and a critic cited rough mouse controls and a thin tutorial
Game does not respect player time: reviewers note most players never field a full roster of max-level heroes, and losing a few heroes means regrinding many low-level dungeons
improvements: Give end-game experience a better path, such as resolve-level XP or easier ways to level heroes, so replacing losses is less of a grind
Relax or remove the hero-too-strong-for-quest restriction so players can farm efficiently
Tune the three-tier structure to feel less padded (one forum suggestion: two tiers plus a max-level run at the Darkest Dungeon)
Reduce the randomness of ambushes, camping attacks, and crit streaks, or offer more counterplay and information beforehand
Better onboarding and in-game information so boss and curio mechanics are not pure trial-and-error; smoother mouse controls
Speed options and less tedious quest pacing (animation speed, map traversal) for respect of player time
unique_things: Psychological stress as a core mechanic alongside hit points, with heroes developing afflictions or virtues that can help or sabotage the party
Rank-based positioning combat in which skills work only from certain slots and move enemies and allies around
Permanent death in a persistent hamlet hub: a roguelite meta-loop of rosters and town upgrades rather than fresh runs
Torchlight and provisions management that raises tension and alters loot and enemy strength
Narrator-driven tone that comments on your successes and failures with a dark sense of humour
Hero quirks and diseases that make each recruit feel like a character rather than a disposable unit
tedious_or_disliked: Repeating near-identical low-level missions to level replacement heroes before high-tier content
Expensive upkeep for stress relief, curing diseases, and removing bad traits that drains gold after every trip
Slow animations and traversal that stretch each quest to 20 minutes or more
Ambushes while camping and unavoidable hallway encounters that can kill high-level heroes
Emotional toll of losing favourite heroes; some players say sessions leave them stressed rather than entertained, and the Butcher's Circus arena was not liked by at least one long-time player
divisive_points: Whether the difficulty is fair: many fans say knowledge and preparation remove most RNG, while detractors say it is about 50% luck
Whether the grind is a satisfying meta-loop or a waste of time; fans defend the economy as part of the tension, critics call it padding
Stress system: loved as innovative storytelling by most, but some find the random acting-out and afflictions infuriating
Loss tolerance: fans see permadeath as the point of the game, others bounce off after losing a high-level hero
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched Jan 2015 after a Kickstarter that raised over $313k; the early period drew complaints that it was too difficult, too random, and unfair, and streamer feedback shaped balance before the Jan 19, 2016 release. Sales reportedly hit 650k in the first week, 1M by Nov 2016 and 2M by Dec 2017 (Wikipedia); estimators put Steam owners at 2 to 5 million and gross revenue around $23.9M (Steam-revenue-calculator estimate, not audited). Ports followed for PS4/Vita, Switch, Xbox One, iOS and Linux; Metacritic platform scores range 80 to 85. DLC: The Crimson Court (2017), The Color of Madness (2018), The Butcher's Circus (2020), and The Fire's Edge (newly listed in Steam data). Some critics felt the ending stumbled by lengthening the game with tougher endgame limits, and the Radiant difficulty and mods are common recommendations to ease the grind.
